note: After a few minutes of the customary B&C blissful vibe, they transition to minor with tasty Barber licks and Magner playing a standard piano patch. They shift back to major and Sammy brings in a halftime reggae beat. A chill jam develops, sounding very much like a Jigsaw Earth intro (Jigsaw would be debuted a few months later on 10/7/99). Barber was clearly feeling this jam, because he starts singing some Hey’s and Whoa’s out of nowhere. Eventually Sammy increases the tempo. Barber teases Voices, and then the full band goes into a mini Voices jam, before Brownie segues into the Basis middle funk section.
The second jam is a pretty strong early type one version, with some excellent Barber preceding the ending riffs.
One of the earliest Magellans to break out of the box. It gets spacey and sinister in the middle before returning to familiar territory and building to a triumphant peak.

A very Magner-dominated trance jam. It begins in a pretty simplistic form, with Magner utilizing the 98 style synths, but he gradually layers in more symphonic effects as the jam builds in intensity. Barber steps to the forefront in the final minutes of the jam, sounding equally like he could be building to the end of Basis or the beginning of Helicopters, before he finally gives away the destination.

A blissful theme develops out of the composition, featuring notable piano presence from Magner. The jam evolves into a trance passage, and explores some sinister territory before returning to the song.
An absolutely evil version, with Magner making notable usage of the Gates of Hell synth.
The main jam is excellent, with a sinister Shimmy-esque build all the way up to the ending.

Some very unconventional setlisting yields this gem of experimental music. There is some distinct Pat & Dex jamming for the first several minutes, as Brownie is very reluctant to relinquish the distinctive bass line, but out of this section Barber and (especially) Magner are able to carve some great atmosphere. A spectacular Magner dominated crescendo over the 12-13 minute mark before the jam melts into Voices territory
Aggressive fast-moving trance that dips for a solid chunk into major-mode territory. As it moves back toward Shimmy there is a brief breakdown into a cacophonous Magner passage.
This strong type one version has some unsettling atmosphere in the middle before the build-up to the ending.

The main jam is mellow and blissful all the way through. Some excellent thematic Barber shredding indicate a strong Radiator ending, but instead of finishing the song, the band fakes out the ending and builds up an Aceetobee intro with meticulous patience.
A ferocious type one version that features some cool riffs from Barber before a pretty clumsy ending.
A somewhat sudden Waves peak and ending concludes this solid early "Waves Like Hell" sandwich.
Very spacey trance gives way to cacophonous weirdness before building to a strong Helicopters ending
Excellent Basis ending on an excellent Basis > Helix > Basis sandwich

A very unconventional Shem-Rah jam. Magner stays predominantly on piano the entire time, and Barber takes the lead, building up to a massive Magellan ending fakeout. After the fakeout the jam breaks down into ambient atmosphere, and slides into a very mellow Vassillios intro.
A monster Run Like Hell ending serves as the landing pad to an excellent Bazaar Escape jam and an exclamation point to a fantastic set.
Ambient lounge trance devolves into minimalist psychedelia that builds back up into a slow and incredibly soulful Mulberry’s intro.

Emerging from the one-off Pygmy riff is this impressive piece of instant type two. Sammy drops to half time almost immediately, and the rest of the band follow, crafting a vaguely dubby trance atmosphere. Towards the end of the jam Sammy quickens the tempo as the band moves toward Dribble. It's a very short jam, but very exploratory.

The normally blissful RLH jam steadily creeps into darker territory. A little shy of the nine minute mark the jam makes a sudden dive into type two, and builds on a Shimmy ending theme, before a very sudden and forced transition back into RLH.

Atmospheric and patient, a harbinger of the more famous Waves that was played next. Magner utilizes a haunting, echoing synth effect and Barber plays simple and complementary riffs. Shortly before the ten minute mark Magner busts out the more droning trance synths, taking lead in the jam until Barber begins to peak it.

Forced to abort mid-jam shortly after the Cyclone composition due to inclement weather, the band took the stage about 45 minutes later and "restarted" Cyclone. After a lightning-fast count from Allen, the band resumes the jam seemingly right where they abruptly ended it. The jam remains high-energy all the way through, moving from a brooding major key theme to triumphant bliss culminating in a Basis ending.

This is the earliest Vassillios outro in circulation. Sammy holds the beat in Vassillios territory while the other three play around with this theme. Magner starts off on the electric organ but by the thirteen minute mark he’s in full-blown trance mode. The jam builds to a chaotic peak before settling into an Aceetobee intro.

On the heels of a groundbreaking version two nights prior, this Helicopters jam begins in much the same way. Magner's repetitive synth lines anchor the jam, giving Barber room to explore. His playing, and the overall tone of the jam, is particularly melancholy much of the way through. The jam builds in intensity, but doesn't definitively move into major key territory until after the track change. Like the jam into it, this Helicopters jam doesn't show its hand until the very end.
It builds to a pretty cool bliss theme and uncomposed peak, but its the masterful segue into Floodlights that is really worth your time.

The Vassillios outro starts off mellow, but builds gradually to a massive uplifting crescendo around the seventeen minute mark. It sounds almost like Run Like Hell territory, or something similarly major-key, before Barber suddenly (but not in a bad way) lays down the Waves riff to signal the transition
The first part of the theme is tense and exploratory, but the second is a fist-pumping conclusion. A contender for strongest standalone version.

Debut. The band carves an impressive jam section out of a relatively rigid composition. Stylistically, the jam begins with some similarities to a Don jam: a kind of blissful driving trance progression. The jam is ambient and atmospheric at times, complemented by the guest violinist, and builds to a pleasant crescendo before Sammy signals the return to EKN.

The jam out of the first jam section begins as very mellow trance, but Magner quickly incorporates the Gates of Hell synth and some of his other abrasive effects. Barber uses a cool distortion that creates an excellent complementary effect. After a tense theme it moves through more blissful territory and then builds up to a sinister crescendo. After a breakdown, it builds up to a short Run Like Hell intro.

The first Overture to feature a jam, and the first foray into Jungle music for the Disco Biscuits. It's a very short jam (only about 90 seconds) but it is an important development for the song nonetheless.

It covers a few different themes but for the most part it stays within the box, taking a brief detour through more tense territory but mostly following along the path of a triumphant and delightful jungle jam.
Great mellow atmosphere and Sister Judy’s-esque vocal jamming.
The ending to a rare split-up Trooper serves as the landing pad to one of the greatest segments of Biscuits bliss improv.

The intro jam is the most interesting of the three, with spacey looping from Barber and layered atmospheric effects.

The main jam is almost completely type one, but stretched out as far as it can go. The mellow atmospheric jam reaches a brief, tense passage before building to the peak.

While both jams are excellent, it is the dub jam that is far more interesting. The lively take on this section is more energetic than typical, dominated by inspired Barber shredding that builds to a monstrous uncomposed peak.

Patient trance gradually builds in intensity. Magner crafts the perfect atmosphere while Barber builds to a mini-crescendo. The jam, as do many of the greats from this year and tour, enters a brief type two dub passage before it begins to build up to a Run Like Hell intro.

Absolutely demented trance. Magner’s synth lines are one-of-a-kind, reminiscent of a video game sound effect. The jam remains in sinister minor-key territory until the final minutes when Brownie drops the Crickets bass line.

The 7-11 jam gets off to a standard start, but soon dissolves into a minor-key trance exploration. Barber pushes the jam into a triumphant major-key theme reminiscent of Helicopters or Basis, which gradually makes its way back into Mulberry’s territory after numerous teases.
Furious raging trance-fusion yields to the more relaxed build of a Run Like Hell intro, complemented excellently by Derhak’s bass.
A strong early iteration that, like many of the Story jams with the Triscuits, stays in more somber territory than usual before building up to the glorious peak.
Jammed out of the first section, which is less intense than usual. Lighthearted mellow trance breaks down into a gorgeous and spacey groove going into Jigsaw.

The first really significant Jigsaw trance jam, and the beginning of the song’s golden age. It is considerably more fleshed out and thematic than previous versions, and it builds to a thrilling uncomposed peak.

A mind bending ambient jam during the slowed down middle of Bazaar sets the tone for this rare, exploratory version. After returning to the composed section, a DnB jam emerges with Magner and Allen leading. Sweeping synth lines and expertly placed e-drum hits are highlights in this high energy section. The tempo and intensity of the jam increase considerably before they smoothly find their way into the ending peak.
The jam covers a wide range of territory, from blissed-out dub rock, to more tense dnb, to a psychedelic caveman rock ending.

The jam pretty quickly leaves traditional Overture dnb territory in favor of a chillout dub passage. A few minutes in, the jam transitions into trance territory, with Magner contributing on the flute patch in an interesting way. The remainder of the jam is an airy trance vehicle that builds to a fantastic Helicopters intro.
A unique version. Where most B&C jams featured a (sometimes extensive) detour through sinister territory, this jam breaks down to an atonal passage before the buildup to familiar territory.

After a standard middle section, the I-Man jam is a very slow burn. it builds on a darker than typical theme with meticulous patience until it descends into utter chaos around the 17 minute mark. From here the jam deconstructs and builds itself back into Shimmy territory for a rousing Shimmy peak
A pretty excellent and experimental Svenghali jam, with an unconventional “peak” in the middle. The segue into Story is solid as well.
A well-executed Waves peak and ending section punctuate the famous Waves > Vassillios > Waves sandwich

Beginning as a standard Don jam with mellow Barber strumming and mildly piercing Magner synths, it breaks down into a stunning orchestral passage, with ambient Magner synths and Barber soundscapes. It settles into a subdued groove, and soon begins the march into Shem-Rah Boo.

A catchy, patient dnb vehicle. The transformation back into trance is smooth. Barber’s playing retains some of the weirdness that characterizes Biscuits’ dnb jams long after the rhythm has shifted toward more traditional trance. The build to the Waves peak is excellent.

Barber and Magner immediately lock into a sinister, hypnotic theme. Around 4:30, Magner introduces the Gates of Hell, the distinctive feature of this version. Barber uses a kind of digital distortion effect on his guitar for the next theme, which is equally hypnotic but far more triumphant. It remains very trancey until Barber takes the lead and builds to a gorgeous Confrontation ending.

Begins with a strong amelodic distortion from Barber, but he soon abandons it in favor of the muted effect he uses during dnb jams. The jam remains in trance territory for a few minutes more until Sammy begins to incorporate breakbeats. Barber signals the drop into Overture early, but thinks better of it and hangs back, allowing the jam to build to a respectable crescendo.

Another powerful standalone dnb vehicle. Barber forms the foundation of the first half of the jam and Magner takes control in the second half. Sammy’s shift in tempo is accompanied by a key change from Magner, and the transition into the ending is smoothly executed.

For a short, set-closing standalone, the Home Alone manages to cover some interesting territory. It dips into a tense, minor-mode theme that goes beyond typical Home Again territory, and remains there up to the peak section.

Two distinct themes, and both top-tier, kick off one of the best segments of the year. The first is pure bliss that builds to a gorgeous, uncomposed, Barber-led crescendo. The second is a pretty typical Vassilios intro theme, but Magner’s work in the last 5 minutes of the track are enough to kick it up a notch.
Evil minimalist trance. Utter Magner domination. All-time Nughuffer jam.
A tense, creeping trance theme that builds to probably the greatest Waves peak ever. https://youtu.be/hx9v_N5jjRY
An expansive and atmospheric jam that quickly leaves behind traditional dnb for a more relaxed, almost dub groove.

Around 4:15 the jam leaves Trooper territory and enters into a moody locomotive trance passage. Around the 9 minute mark Magner dramatically shifts the tone of the synths to a more abrasive and cacophonous style. The jam enters a passage of chaotic and psychedelic music, with Magner blending a rapid fire electric organ with his most heavily electronic trance synths, all punctuated by a thunderous repeating bass riff from Brownie. This portion of the jam builts to a fever pitch until just after the 16 minute mark, when the rhythm section begins to drop the tempo down to what is distinctly an Aceetobee intro.
A fantastic use of minimalist space, especially from Magner. A great sinister type two theme reaches an unconventional crescendo and returns to Crickets territory.

Monster show-opening 32-minute version. This is an all-around great I-Man, but the highlight is the 2nd jam. Right off the bat, Brownie comes up with a nifty staccato riff, while Barber and Magner create a blissful soundscape. Allen transitions into a halftime dub feel. After a few minutes of this chill airy vibe, they do a 180 and shift into the parallel minor for an in-your-face dirty dub jam. Rockstar Barber wails on the guitar while Allen deploys some aggressive fills, backed by Magner and Brownie playing in unison. And suddenly Barber plays his composed descending I-Man lick over this evil dub jam, and it is a perfect transition back into the parallel major for a great I-Man ending.

The Humu outro drops straight into Aceetobee middle territory, and seems to portend a perfunctory jam. Not so. The riff breaks down into several tense ambience and builds to an unconventional crescendo. Barber makes great use of the fall 2000 style phaser.
The rare intro jam sets this Bazaar Escape apart from the pack.

After very standard first and second jams, the outro catapults the listener into outer space. Barber locks into a complementary theme almost immediately, and filters it through a cool “underwater” effect.

After stronger-than-usual intro and mid-verse jams, the main jam is an ethereal beauty. It stays pretty close to Floes territory, but pushes that space further when we’ve seen it go yet, and foreshadows the more expansive fall versions.
The Magner-dominated acid jazz jam begins to break down around the ten minute mark into ambient weirdness. Barber takes over and links up with Magner in the final minutes for an excellent conclusion.

The blissful Aceetobee theme takes on a more haunting quality, with excellent atmospheric synths and a strong bass line. The tense theme comes to a head until the track change, where it steadily shifts into Confrontation bliss.
A characteristically strong spring 01 version, it explores a tense, dub passage before returning to the triumphant ending.

An adventurous, unconventionally tense first jam even manages to find its way away from the Very Moon bass line for a few minutes. 

The second jam soon breaks away from staid Very Moon funk and launches into a thematic masterpiece. Two distinct themes lead the jam through a triumphant passage to more settled melancholia before a smooth segue into Pygmy.
Both jams are solidly “type one plus,” but Barber’s has a nice spaced out section and one of the more iconic Mulberry’s peaks out there.
Standard Waves trance breaks down into an unconventional passage with Magner on the marimba patch and rebuilds into a stellar Waves peak.
A mellow dub jam with very "soundy" Magner effects dominating the sound profile. Barber builds it to an unconventional crescendo and Sammy quickly kicks up the tempo for the transition into Dribble.
Somewhat lumbering, introspective trance. There are a few passages where the tempo shifts to a slightly slower pace, but overall this is a steady, singular build to a Helicopters intro.
Not fully type two, like many of the all-timers from this tour, but the first jam nevertheless has an enjoyable “deconstructed type one.”
27min improvisational jam

The jam remains in bliss territory, but still manages to leave behind the most restrictive confines of Spacebird for a long theme.

A tense and brooding trance jam emerges in the Spacebird outro, building to an explosive Helicopters peak.
A cool, evil dnb theme, highlighted by the 11/9 synths, that melts back into a strong Mulberry’s ending.
Skull crushing dnb. Even in a tour replete with jungle, this jam manages to stand out. The jam smoothly departs Mulberry’s territory and moves from a blissful dnb vehicle to a sinister peak.
Another of the top-shelf September Sound 1s, vying with 9/6, 9/12 and 9/15. This version is the most sinister of the month, with multiple evil themes and peaks before returning to Sound 1.
Fast-paced, atmospheric trance yields to a slower and more patient groove. The groove builds patiently to a Dribble intro.
Patient atmospheric grooves build to a raging dnb conclusion.

The trance jam begins with a feather light, airy trance theme from Magner, and is pushed forward by an excellent Barber/Sammy cooperation. It builds to an absolutely furious peak before returning to the chase section.
The band takes their time leaving Triumph territory, builds up a blissful dnb theme, and finally settles into Ape territory.
A pretty dub-heavy Hope, balancing the dnb-heavy jams earlier in the segment. Magner develops great blissful flute patch lines that gradually build to a gorgeous conclusion.
The mid-chase jam is psychedelic and thematic, evocative of interstellar travel. It builds to a massive peak which leads to a DJ segue into Munchkin.
Magner utilizes his most acidic acid synths even as the tempo gradually drops towards Hope. Great, grimy trance.

The jam coalesces around a very simple but haunting bass line. It explores a variety of territory—from sinister Shimmy-esque trance, to haunting Munchkin-esque breaks, to a near-fakeout of Aquatic Ape—all before returning to another Confrontation peak.
Though not as exploratory or deep as the September versions, the jam features a great spacey theme in the first half with very tasteful atmospheric synth work.

The jam begins by exploring the space around the ending of the Story peak riff, but moves into the sinister territory typical of a Shimmy jam a few minutes in. Pretty soon, we are in a full-blown minor-key trance jam. There is a steady build to bliss territory, and a massive Confrontation peak.
The outro jam has a blissful dnb theme that crests a wave and breaks down to Hope ending territory.

Emerging out of the middle section of I-Man, the jam sees Magner make use of a synth palette that harkens back to the great Aceetobee intros of September. The jam reaches a phenomenal and very tense groove with an array of distorted synth effects and settles comfortably into Aceetobee type one.

This monster version (one of the longest standalone versions ever) has a strong main jam that ventures beyond Voices territory. Unlike the fall 00 greats, which tend toward the sinister and the melancholy, this version is life-affirming and gorgeous.
The jam stays in Very Moon territory before a tempo shift (accompanied by Rivers of Babylon teases). The buildup to the 7-11 ending is steady and lovely.

The mid-verse jam is sparse and sinister, and very out of the ordinary. The tempo changes and the band briefly explores a demented groove. Short, but very worth hearing.

The main jam reaches a sinister theme and yields a massive Run Like Hell peak.

Fairly standard at first, with distorted trance synths coalescing into a triumphant theme. It begins to move toward tense territory, and shortly thereafter Magner goes absolutely wild on the Gates of Hell synth. After he eases up, the jam actually explores some cool territory, before making its return to Munchkin.
Begins with the usual sinister trance, but breaks down into contemplative, near-ambient melancholy. It builds in intensity as it reaches Boop.

Great even for the era. The theme is powerful and brooding, and the rhythm section offers enough variety to keep things interesting. The minor-key build to the ending suggests a possible inverted Overture, but the return to the peak feels very natural.
A strong trance theme with a mellow breakdown before a buildup into the first-ever Inverted Ladies.
The main jam launches into a great bliss theme after a few short minutes, but gradually breaks down into more ambient space with a more melancholy atmosphere.
Sprawling and formless at first, the jam eventually coalesces around a steadily building bliss theme.

After a raucous intro jam, the main jam is nearly fifteen minutes long. Some four on the floor from Sammy, with occasional but minimal variation, forms the backbone of this excellent early Basis. As Magner layers on a range of his old school 1998 style synths, Barber plays a series of light airy riffs that keep the jam moving along briskly. The jam builds to a chaotic frenzy before breaking down around the eighteen minute mark into what almost sounds like an I-Man intro. The next few minutes are based around an uplifting synth theme from Magner that gives way around the twenty minute mark. to more involved playing from Barber. The remaining 5-6 minutes of the jam are an extremely patient build to the Basis peak

The first real exploration of the first jam section in Mulberry’s. It quickly pushes the limits of the song structure, with Magner layering ambient synths, and Barber playing atmospheric riffs, while essentially remaining type one. The jam soon breaks into type two, with a great trance theme that quickly enters breakbeat territory. Magner plays the Mulberry’s middle over the Spaga ending rhythm, and the jam finally settles into Spaga.
Fun and playful dnb jamming, with a raging psychedelic theme that builds up to a gorgeous and blissful Shelby ending
Although Brownie never strays far from the House Dog bass line, the jam is still plenty experimental, with a stretched out droning space jam in the middle.
The jam takes on a spacey, tense quality before building up to a Basis fakeout that breaks down into Hope bliss.

Magner’s subdued synth lines take center stage of this minimalist jam. Sammy intersperses some slower grooves in with the breakbeats, until he eventually shifts the tempo toward M.E.M.P.H.I.S. The jam retains the melancholy disposition of Spaga until it reaches a crescendo and breaks down.
Melancholy acid trance yields to percussive rock with a huge peak into the middle section of I-Man.

A banner version. It begins as spacey and very digital trance, with Magner crafting a theme that he weaves deftly through an organically shifting rhythm section that vacillates between trance and dub. In the second half, the tempo becomes more regular, and settles into a steady theme before returning to Shem.
A melancholy undercurrent runs through this usually blissful section.

A mind-expanding 42. The jam evolves first into a symphonic theme, with Magner and Barber in sync, before it breaks down into a psychedelic passage characterized by Allen's regular e-drum beat and percussive xylophone synths from Magner. Barber latches onto a catchy riff that he patiently builds on for the rest of the jam, eventually leading into the end of 42. A pinnacle of the setbreak era, and considered by some to be the greatest 42 ever played.
Fast-paced trance descends into mellow ambience and segues into Spacebird.

The beginning of the track is all Mauricio. It is hard to say exactly when the band joins in, but by 5:15 you can clearly hear Magner and Sammy. Magner and Mauricio together create quite an interesting sound (a portent of things to come), and they craft a haunting theme. The theme comes to a head around the eleven minute mark. Magner plays these haunting descending synth lines, and around this time Mauricio leaves and Brownie takes the stage. The jam enters a more blissed out passage as the dust settles. At 14:15 the mood shifts considerably darker, and a loud cheer indicates that Barber has taken the stage (he can be heard shortly after). A total musical breakdown follows. The mood of the ensuing theme is almost playful. Barber plays around on a vaguely eastern sounding scale, and Magner's synth effect is reminiscent of a sitar. This theme begins to give way to another around the 24 minute mark. It's more focused and traditional sounding, and more somber. Around 28 the theme breaks down again and Magner comes back with the sitar-esque synth briefly. The jam develops into something of a good-natured, lumbering beast. It builds up to a small peak around 32 and then breaks down again. The theme that develops here is determined and forceful, and the Helix teases around 35:30 only add to that mood. Barber is on a mission. Another breakdown at 37:40 and Sammy immediately lays down a short-lived dub line. Some chaos (and another Star Wars tease from Magner?) and then a very gradual build. Elements of dub and rock in the ensuing build to the first "real" crescendo of the Akira Jam. Barber from 43:20 on is magnificent. Breakdown at 45:40 and the jam goes into space. The jam moves toward more mellow territory around the four minute mark of the second track. Some incredibly patient, focused, triumphant jamming develops over the next four minutes. After another breakdown the jam that develops is a weird mix of chaotic and frenzied (from the rhythm section) and pleasantly peaceful (from the melody). The mood shifts, and the jam becomes more purposeful and cinematic, and builds up to another energetic peak. Breaks down again, with more hints of dub until Sammy starts going all over the map. It settles down around the eighteen minute mark, and, like many themes on the second track, is vaguely sinister and very purposeful. Around 22:30 the band settles into an actual dub theme. It is totally demented, the epitome of what some call "pirate trance." The band keeps the mood and momentum as they transition back into more typical trancefusion. One last breakdown just shy of thirty minutes. The final buildup is slow, more patient and restrained than you might expect given the eventual destination. It hits a lull then begins to build up around 37. The key change comes very smoothly, and the climb up to theBasis peak is patiently arduous. The GAYFM section is the most extended version yet. It breaks down into a blissful groove and slides smoothly into the second peak.

The mid-verse jam goes unconventionally deep. Brownstein dives almost immediately into dub territory, before the jam heads into sparse trance. It builds to a Shimmy fakeout before returning to Run Like Hell.
A short-lived but gorgeous theme develops out of the Helicopters composition. It builds to an unconventional crescendo and -> to the Jigsaw chase riff.
A very nice, drawn-out type one theme, complemented and accentuated by some traditional fall 01 effects from Barber.

7-11 returns to the catalog after nearly a year of absence and quickly establishes itself as a trance-fusion powerhouse. The pace never slackens, and the jam builds from barely restrained ferocity to a crushing Basis peak.
Though it is more blissful than many of the spring versions, there is nevertheless a strong Magner presence to this Munchkin that gives the jam a distinctly F2K feel.

After a perfect segue from the Crickets jam, they settle into Voices nicely. Adding textural riffs to the composed section of the song, there’s little doubt they’re about to soar as the jam begins. Mellow and patient, Magner’s and Barber’s melodies swirl and chase one another, as Marc and Allen move things along with purpose. Magner introduces the signature theme of the jam around 10:30, and the rest of the band crafts their parts around its ascending beauty. Barber’s lines are tasteful and gorgeous in their own right, and genius e-drum fills from Allen (using the talking drum patch) tie things together nicely. The sounds each member creates are interwoven, but somehow they give each other the perfect amount of space. After the jam reaches its pinnacle, the band confidently downshifts, slowing things way down, until they finally land seamlessly in Rainbow song.
Melancholy build, percussive breakdown, and a fantastic type two crescendo before returning to the familiar peak.
Most of the jam is deftly restrained tension. It spills over the sides in a somewhat weird passage in the middle, but it builds to a thrilling peak.
A gorgeous, blissful trance vehicle with Munchkin Invasion flavor and teases. It builds to an unconventionally blissful Dribble ending.
A gorgeous, mellow, and blissful outro moves at a relaxed pace towards Hope. It never reaches a real crescendo, but instead breaks down into an unconventional dnb passage before the Hope intro.
The main jam has a vaguely Bazaar Escape sounding portion that gives a more forceful, determined air to a usually blissful jam section. There’s a cool type two breakdown and return to the peak.
A Barber-led dnb vehicle in which he develops a great theme almost immediately and drives it up through a number of cool effects to a comparably mellow crescendo.

A very ahead-of-its-time Boop with two important jams. The first jam is considerably more thematic than was typical of a first Boop jam of the time, but still features plenty of Magner showing off. The breakdown around 6:30 right before the peak is particularly fun.

The second jam, likewise, is more thematic than usual. It begins with the typical format of a Barber blues solo with Magner on clav, but gradually begins to incorporate more electronic synths. The interplay in the final minutes is fantastic. The jam remains type one, but it is nevertheless an important development for Boop.

Another fall 01 Triumph that explores every possible pocket of type 1 before moving on. The breakdown into Vassilios territory is very smooth, and the uncomposed peak before the drop into the song is fantastic.

The first "unfinished" Very Moon, and one that would set the stage for that song's development. Around the eleven minute mark the jam shows every sign of heading toward the ending, but Magner introduces trance synths, playing the standard ending riff as the jam gradually begins to break away from the structure. From here we are treated to a much more fleshed out exploration of this section. At sixteen minutes the jam is definitely in Voices territory, and the band revamps the jam for a gorgeous psychedelic Voices intro.

The first jam is notable for the considerable presence of trance synths. It remains type one, but has that added layer to make it more interesting than usual.

The main jam begins with a drum solo that leads into a lengthy and soulful Mulberry's jam. Like the first jam, it's still type one, but it is one of the most thorough explorations of this section.

An outro jam emerges before the last verse and Waves riff, maintaining the locomotive momentum of Bazaar. The jam instantly breaks down into type two weirdness, with busy Barber riffing and unconventional synth effects from Magner. He incorporates a rave synth around the twelve minute mark, but by 13:30 the jam is all bliss. Excellent theme construction in this section. The band manages to not show their hand for several minutes, but by 16:30 it's pretty clear that this has become a Run Like Hell jam.
A fiery Shimmy peak serves as the exclamation point to an exploratory I-Man jam
A cool bliss theme coming out of the Aceetobee intro that slides into darker territory as it approaches The Overture.

A monolithic Magner-dominated trance jam emerges out of the Vassillios outro. Sinister themes pervade the jam until around the 14 minute mark, when Barber begins leading back into the bliss territory of B&C

Probably the only Barber-on-bass jam that didn’t feel like musical treading water. The jam doesn’t always click, and is almost always incohesive, but the experimental factor alone makes it worthwhile.

After a very standard first jam, the second jam immediately makes a dive into type two territory (the first such occurrence within Aceetobee). Brooding and dark, the jam follows this monolithic theme until it abruptly (and not in a negative way) drops back into Aceetobee.
Quickly departs Sven dnb in favor of more of a rock groove. After a breakdown reminiscent of a Story or M.E.M.P.H.I.S. intro, the jam begins to build up to a Run Like Hell intro.
Voices had been steadily incorporating longer atmospheric jams since fall 1999, and this is a culmination of that progression.

A Barber-dominated shuffling trance theme unfolds over the first several minutes. Magner contributes his synth waves, adding atmosphere. Around the 12-13 minute mark, their roles shift; Barber plays a steady background riff and Magner takes lead on the trance synths. In the closing minutes of the jam, Barber and Magner team up to build a massive peak.
The I-Man outro moves through many moods until what is almost a Dribble fakeout before settling into a type one Fiddler ending.
Another strong mid-verse jam, it begins in tense, grungey territory, with Barber using heavy distortion, and builds to another strong Run Like Hell jam.

A determined, repeating riff from Barber underscores this melancholy masterpiece. Magner makes effective use of fall 2000 style synths in crafting the somber atmosphere, and Barber gradually pushes the jam back into Munchkin territory.
The longest Sound 1 of September is a great exercise in patience. It may feel a bit bloated at times, but the patience is ultimately rewarded.
Very mellow trance settles into a hypnotic groove after a few minutes. After a breakdown it builds back up to a much more easygoing pace and then picks the tempo back up into Vassilios territory.

Some pretty standard B&C bliss jamming that gradually slows down, as Magner sneaks in with some distinctly Magellan-esque piano. He hooks up with Sammy and Brownie in the final minute before the segue, which is as smooth as you could ask for

A pretty standard ambient trance jam emerges from Helicopters, but by the 4 minute mark Magner has locked into an infectiously catchy theme on the flute patch. He stays predominantly on the flute patch for most of the rest of the jam, allowing Barber to contribute complementary riffs. After a chaotic crescendo around 9:30, the jam settles down into a Trooper intro
A trance jam gradually emerges out of the oft-underutilized Aceetobee middle. A patient build to the Waves peak follows.
Swirling psychedelia that ventures away, but never strays too far, from B&C type one
Some cool percussive stop/start jamming yields a drawn-out blissful dnb jam. It gradually shifts into minor-key territory for an excellent segue into Waves.

Magner's droning synths give the Worcester jam some continuity from the preceding Nughuffer jam. Here they no longer sound sinister, but uplifting, and Barber's distinct guitar riffs add to this atmosphere. After some exploration, Barber settles into a distinct (and vaguely dubby) theme around the three minute mark that carries through the rest of the jam. In the final minutes of this jam, the theme gradually picks up speed for an impressive segue into Mindless Dribble

The jam begins as standard Nughuffer trance but gradually gives way to an eerie theme dominated by Magner's droning synths. The backbone of this theme remains relatively unchanged as it builds to a terrific crescendo that breaks down heading to the famous "Worcester Jam"

A distinctly mellow Waves trance theme makes up the first half, and some spectacular work from Sammy characterizes the second half. After a crescendo and breakdown, Sammy lays the groundwork for some fun hip-hop jamming that breaks down into some jungle fills before returning to Mulberry’s.

After a standard first jam, the outro starts off ambient and atmospheric, with Magner's choral synths serving as the backdrop for the jam. Barber comes in with alternating ascending/descending riffs, and Magner follows him with a complementary synth line. Sammy pushes the tempo faster while Magner locks into a repetitive riff that gives Barber the space to play around with some bluesy riffs. Around 13 minutes in Brownie begins to signal the segue. Magner stays locked in a trance groove as Barber builds up to an excellent Basis drop

A great early Helicopters jam which begins with Magner playing around with a very digital synth. Barber noodles for a bit but locks into a great theme with Magner around 4:30. They build on this theme for most of the jam, but it breaks down by the ten minute mark and rebuilds into an excellent Run Like Hell intro

A hypnotic trance jam that incorporates some breakbeat flourishes as the theme breaks down into a slower groove, before building back up to a large crescendo that melts into a News From Nowhere intro.
After a slow start, the band settles into a gorgeous theme that yields an effortless segue into Story.

Another typically strong 99 Dribble. Magner does a spectacular job of crafting somber atmosphere, and Barber’s soulful licks are the perfect complement. The first Dribble hits come in around 7:30 and Barber gradually takes the lead. As the ferocity builds, Barber delivers an absolute scorcher of a peak, enhanced by Magner’s demented synth work.

Only the third Dribble outro of the year, and the one responsible for making it a staple of the catalogue. A chaotic jam emerges with Magner mostly relying on the piano and Barber playing a simple three note pattern over Sammy’s furious drumming. Barber takes the lead and builds to a fantastic Basis peak.

And now for something completely different: this nearly six minute breakbeat Dribble intro is a direct precursor to the 11/9 set two opening jam, and doesn’t sound like a single Dribble intro before or since.

Though it begins with a standard Dribble groove, the main jam quickly gets weird. Magner moves toward more experimental effects, and Sammy lays down a four on the floor trance beat. A rare type two Dribble.

Significant for being the first jam to feature both Mauricio and a drummer, the Helicopters jam is much more energetic than previous Mauricio jams. Magner dominates the first theme, and then Barber builds the jam to an excellent Waves peak.

A jam (the first of any kind out of Bazaar Escape) develops around the Waves riff at the end of Bazaar. Barber holds on to the riff for the first minute of jamming, and plays around with similar sounding ideas for another minute. Here Sammy and Brownie begin to change up the tempo, quickening the jam. Magner stays on the piano until around the 4 minute mark, and here the jam is completely an Aceetobee intro. Barber plays around with some jazzy licks for another few minutes before dropping the Aceetobee riff
A strong bookend to the Helicopters > Run Like Hell > Helicopters sandwich

In contrast to the jam into it, the jam out of Run Like Hell sees Magner make liberal use of the 1998 synths. The early part of the jam sounds not unlike the 12/30/98 Nughuffer jam. Barber's playing is very minimalist and atmospheric; it is Magner who leads the way at first. Barber becomes more involved around the 13 minute mark, and joins in a chaotic breakdown of the previous theme from 14-16 minutes. From out of this chaos Barber leads the band into a gorgeous Helicopters peak

A watershed version of Shimmy, which departs from the traditionally dark Shimmy territory for some considerably more uplifting jamming. This version shaped the way Shimmy was played for the rest of the tour and beyond.
Although another version of this segment was played three days prior, it's quite different. Magner makes liberal use of 1998 synths, and the build to the RLH bliss peak is very steady and deliberate.

Another type two RLH jam, and very different from the version from three days prior. Sammy drops the tempo noticeably, and the jam moves through a passage of dub groove. The relaxed portion is short-lived, and by the seven minute mark the band is pretty firmly back in a Run Like Hell jam. After a breakdown around the ten minute mark, the jam very briefly dips into more sinister territory before making the climb back to RLH.
The jam traverses a chaotic breakdown as it moves from dubby trance to breakbeats. The band builds to a strong crescendo which loses no steam as it slams into The Overture.

An absolutely thrilling Dribble. The beginning of the jam is patient to an even greater degree than typical. Magner's ambient, droning synths add a haunting atmosphere, and Barber works with extreme patience to craft the perfect riffs (check out his work beginning around the nine minute mark). He builds the jam to a fiery but still thematic conclusion.

The sharply focused jam leaves the acid jazz territory of a traditional Pygmy jam almost immediately. Around the five minute mark, Magner locks onto a short and simple riff that the band builds into a massive theme. The explosive "Bad Love" crescendo takes the place of the traditionally uncomposed peak, and the band drops shortly thereafter into the end of Pygmy.

A fantastic, Magner-led trance jam, with the whole band locks into a catchy theme immediately. The Gates of Hell make a rare appearance. The trance breaks down into ambience before rebuilding into a steady groove that leads into M.E.M.P.H.I.S. territory.
Moves into a lengthy, tense theme before returning to one of the strongest Crickets peaks yet.
The jam quickly leaves the most constrictive Spacebird territory, and settles into a sinister Barber-led theme. It gradually settles into a massive Basis intro.

What is usually a Barber solo is an excuse for him to show off so much more. Tempo and rhythm changes abound, all tied together by Barber’s screaming guitar work. After a couple minutes, the jam settles into a dub-adjacent jam with weird vocalizations from Barber and rabbit hole synths from Magner. It builds to a thoroughly disgusting uncomposed peak, and breaks down into Spacebird territory from there.
1st and only split Abraxas really shows the bands ability for improvising any song as this jam & whole segment is excellent with a triumphant return to Abraxas after 3 great classic songs in between.
Terrific return to Abraxas out of a M.E.M.P.H.I.S Jam this whole segment is definitely something fans of improvisation & Abraxas should listen to.
A mellow and mournful Magner theme gradually gives way to a chaotic Barber peak. The minimalist portions are the strongest, but it’s a solid version overall.

A magnificent soundscape. The traditional jungle style jam leaves the poppy bliss of Svenghali almost instantly, as Barber plays the signature riff through a variety of effects. Barber uses a heavily muted distortion effect as he settles into a theme, and he and Magner craft an unsettling atmosphere. The first theme builds in to a chaotic crescendo that leads to a fake-out of the Overture ending. After this, Barber's tone is noticeably cleaner. He gradually brings Magner out of the abyss of darkness, and the pair lead into a blissful Svenghali ending.

It takes a while to get there, but by the nine minute mark the band is locked into a gorgeous mellow groove. Brownie begins signalling the move to RLH around the twelve minute mark, and the rest of the jam is a build to a powerful RLH intro.

First jam starts off fairly standard, if a little restrained. Magner's bass synth is very prominent. The jam seems to be quickly moving towards a standard peak, but Magner's cooing bird synths signal a departure from the norm, and shortly after, around 6:30, the jam begins to break down. Barber immediately takes on a more prominent role, and signals a move toward more sinister territory. Magner follows suit shortly after. In the ensuing minutes, Barber and Magner are so in step with each other they almost sound like a single unit. The jam breaks down once again and moves through another sinister theme, gradually returning to Boop territory
Excellent Barber work in this one. About six minutes of fairly standard though solid Don jamming reaches a Don ending fakeout before a sudden breakdown and drawn out return into Bazaar territory.

After some jazzy electronic synths from Magner, the band rapidly settles into a Barber-led theme. Barber's playing is extremely clean and focused, and the thematic build results in one of the better recent Spacebird endings.

After a few minutes of standard shredding, the jam breaks down into a somewhat predictable HAB groove, expansive and atmospheric. It becomes really interesting, however, when Sammy completely breaks down the tempo, and the jam spends several minutes building its way back up into a Plan B intro.
Some excellent work by Magner in the first jam, in which he moves from organ to piano and back to organ for the conclusion.

A very strong type two B&C. Magner locks in to a haunting theme very soon after the jam departs from bliss territory, and he holds it with minimal variation for several minutes. The jam breaks down into some very weird, eerie type two in the middle, sounding somewhat like a Vassillios intro. Around 14:30 the jam very steadily begins to climb back into bliss territory as it returns to B&C.

Like the debut, it is essentially a 7-11 jam until it's not, but the early 7-11 jams are such a distinctive sound that we can't really fault this. The theme is considerably better developed here, and the transition into a Boop jam is handled much more adeptly.

The jam begins as very mellow Waves trance. Magner and Barber are both at first feather-light with their playing. Magner locks into a simple catchy theme as Barber noodles, but by the eight minute mark they are both more locked in: Magner has developed an almost cinematic theme, and Barber's playing is more focused as well. The jam stays in very mellow territory, with some soulful Barber playing, until around the 14 minute mark where it sounds like it could be heading back to Waves. Shortly after the 16 minute mark though, the jam abruptly breaks down and shifts to a Run Like Hell intro. The Run Like Hell intro is extremely ambient and atmospheric, and the buildup to the intro is more relaxed than typical.

The jam starts off very slowly, and builds on mellow bliss themes throughout. The bliss themes build to a strong crescendo almost in the vein of a Run Like Hell fake-out, before returning in the final seconds to Above the Waves territory.

Covering tremendous ground, the jam begins with some tasteful Barber/Magner interplay before giving way to a blitz of acid synths. After the eight minute mark the jam mellows out considerably, but Sammy's four on the floor beat keeps things moving forward. A simple trance line from Magner underscores the lamenting cries of Barber's guitar. After a second crescendo at 13:30, the jam dissolves into haunting atmosphere, breaks down, and rebuilds with extreme patience into a Hope intro.
The main jam of this Basis more than makes up for its disappointing intro. A solid stretch of somber jamming breaks down to a minimalist trance passage and rebuilds as a triumphant Basis ending

After an experimental (and somewhat rough) intro jam in which the band makes liberal use of their new toy—a vocal looper/delay device described earlier in the show—the band launches into a fifteen minute main jam: An ethereal and spacey psychedelic journey that covers tremendous ground. A standard, if eminently patient, Run Like Hell jam builds up until the fifteen minute mark where the tone of the jam becomes distinctly somber. The jam breaks down around the eighteen minute mark and begins rebuilding to the Run Like Hell ending. Barber's playing towards the end of the jam is spectacular.
The shortest Basis in over a year, but the main jam doesn't suffer too much for it. It's considerably more straightforward than most Basis jams of the era, but it has the energy to make up for it.
It’s hard to pinpoint exactly when Sammy shifts styles from dnb to trance, but the result of this combination is one of the more well-executed Waves peaks, and one of the more atmospheric dnb jams.

The theme that forms in the first part of the jam is utterly captivating. Once the Dribble hits finally come in, the jam builds to a frenzied Dribble ending. Probably Barber’s best Dribble ending since 3/27/99.

The jam out is a cacophonous trance jam that breaks down in the final minutes into what sounds distinctly like a Crater intro. From here the jam rebuilds into a bliss theme, building to a crescendo that culminates in a powerful Shimmy ending.

The Jigsaw outro is based around the intro/ending riff, which quickly breaks down into structureless noise. Sammy begins to rebuild the thunderous drumming typical of a Floes ending and Barber plays a few pleasant noodling riffs. Magner soon reenters the picture, and pretty soon the jam has taken on a surreal symphonic quality as it builds to the Floes ending.
The perfect example of what a Vassilios jam should sound like, this slow building trance vehicle sounds downright evil before the fist pumping transition into Boop.

The jam begins with Magner on the vocoder and some gorgeous riffs form Barber based around repeating series of triplets, all over Sammy’s thunderous percussion. Barber takes a step out of the box, and then returns to the same theme, building upon it as the band slowly shifts away from the bliss territory of Floes towards the more sinister Jigsaw.

Simply spectacular. Very spacey with extreme patience, and great communication between Magner and Barber. Magner utilizes this repetitive echoing synth line that ebbs and flows like the waves in the sea, and Barber's soulful riff is the perfect complement. Barber's playing in the ending is excellent.
A rare utilization of Fiddler, which yields a thrilling trance theme that culminates in a glorious Aceetobee ending.

Barber lays down a few tense grooves, and Magner mostly stays in the background, contributing occasional Gates of Hell flourishes, until he takes the lead decisively with a hypnotic trance line. Shortly after, Barber takes lead with an ascending riff theme that builds to an excellent peak

The Spaga DnB jam starts off with a somber tone for the first few minutes. Magner with some strange sound effects. They transition to major mode for a blissful airy vibe. Magner uses a flute patch and teases The Beatles’ “Baby You’re a Rich Man,” while Barber adds flavors of House Dog. After peaking this bliss jam, they shift gears entirely and go to the relative minor for a menacing sound. Barber uses a distortion filter, Magner with psychedelic ambiance, Allen with a punishing bass drum pulse. The band is locked in for this evil groove. After several minutes of this aggressive fast tempo, they briefly go into halftime for a more chill dub feel. Allen goes double-time again as the darkness returns and the intensity builds. Magner’s sustained notes signal that the Waves peak is coming. Barber now uses a clean tone for some groovy soloing. Suddenly the band shifts to major for a brief triumphant moment, then go back to minor as Barber wails and they drop into the Waves peak.

Kamaole jam starts out with an energetic happy dancey groove for the first few minutes. They transition to the relative minor for a darker sentiment. Allen gradually slows the tempo down to a hip-hop beat, with a groovy Brownie bassline, and Magner providing a hypnotic atmospheric soundscape. They go into a Robots-esque dark funk jam for the next few minutes. Barber finds a cool repetitive riff as Magner and Brownie transition to a lighter feel. After Barber wails for a bit, he uses a muddy pitch-shifting effect that descends his sustained note over several measures, and at just the right time, the other 3 members drop an out-of-nowhere segue into the 7-11 middle “towel” jam!

Atmospheric and patient dnb with a strong conclusion.

The second jam is, for maybe the first time, the main attraction, with an infectious, mournful synth theme.
Despite the relatively short length, this jam is both exploratory and playful, making a rare segue into the beginning of Waves.

The first jam with the full band since 1999 is probably the highlight of the second set. A standard trance theme breaks down after only a few minutes, and the jam rebuilds itself around Sammy’s breakbeats for a strong Svenghali ending.

An excellent early Shimmy, with Magner anchoring the atmosphere for Barber's haunting riffs. After some absolutely chaotic synth choices around the 11 minute mark, Barber builds the jam to a fiery conclusion

The jam starts off unassumingly, but by the middle the band, led by Magner, finds an infectiously catchy theme. The band builds from this theme into a more triumphant passage, which peaks and begins to build back up to Boop.

At the time the longest Dribble main jam played, this was also probably the first to hint at the song's awesome potential in 1999. Thematic riffs from Barber are underscored by eerie atmospheric synths from Magner, who mostly stays on the flute patch but occasionally punctuates the jam with piercing trance synths. The first Dribble hits come in around 9:30, and mark the beginning of a massive crescendo that explodes in a fiery peak around the fifteen minute mark
The pinnacle of post fall-2000 dnb. In a word, sublime.
Two-part dnb jam, with each part boasting monstrous peaks.

Features chugging sludgy riff from Barber and some haunting synth lines from Magner. Barber shifts to a heavily distorted psychedelic effect, which he will use to great effect in the 11/9/00 Jigsaw. The jam stays in this demented territory for the rest of the track, building to a frenetic pace as the band builds up to an excellent Svenghali ending.

The first jam sees Magner move from organ to trance synths. He plays with a passion, and around 4:45 locks into a spacey theme that he extends and builds up to the peak.

The second jam begins as usual, but quickly develops an unconventional quality. Barber alternates between jazzy riffs and haunting, almost dissonant themes. In the second half of the jam, Barber develops a theme based around a distinct riff, and builds up to a raging conclusion. An excellent early Boop.

A traditional blissful GIG jam, this is not. Immediately an introspective feel develops, with some glitchy/bubbly/static FX in the background. Things take a darker tone with an ambient airy soundscape from Magner, while Allen keeps the beat grooving. A little Pimp Blue Rikkis teasing from Magner. The overall quiet feel of this jam begins patiently transitioning to a fuller sound. Barber takes the lead as they amp up the energy for the GIG peak.

An absolute masterpiece, and contender for the best Dribble of all time. The main jam begins unassumingly, with a repeating synth line over a backdrop of mostly ambient noodling. The rhythm is pretty standard, but Sammy tosses in an occasional breakbeat measure or two. As the Dribble hits come in after a few minutes, Barber takes on more of a leading role, laying down a very catchy repeating riff. After settling into a more mellow passage, the jam begins to build to a crescendo. Sammy’s drumming becomes thunderous, Barber’s playing becomes more ominous, and Magner’s synths take on the quality of drills boring holes into your skull. After a fakeout of the ending, the jam breaks down completely into a second, thoroughly type two theme. Magner crafts a tense atmosphere with a very subtle synth effect. After a further breakdown, Barber takes the lead. He utilizes the muted distortion to great effect, and shortly afterward Magner switches to a heavily electronic synth, reminiscent of a laser beam. After about 4 minutes, Barber switches back to a more regular effect, and builds up to a devastating Dribble ending.

The outro jam features liberal acid synth usage, and toes the line between creepy and uplifting, until a tense breakdown places it firmly in creepy territory. Barber’s riffs take on a decidedly more melancholy quality as Magner’s synths become more foreboding. Sammy begins to increase the tempo, and Magner moves to a more distorted synth effect, as the jam approaches Boop territory.

Like most 01 versions the Helicopters is hardly exploratory, but after a few minutes it settles into an infectious trance theme. It spends a good amount of time in Spacebird-adjacent territory before melting into the song.

The first M.E.M.P.H.I.S. jam to break out of the box, and the one that set the stage for the monumental version the next night. It begins with a mellower energy than any M.E.M.P.H.I.S. before it, despite Sammy's more frantic drum work. The jam stays in this mellow, spacey territory the whole way through, and rather than peaking it melts back into the ending of M.E.M.P.H.I.S.
Mellifluous bliss trance with a massive Barber peak.
The standard Magellan jam transforms organically into a busy, Barber-led groove. It reaches a blissful crescendo and slows down into a 7-11 intro.

Brooding and melancholic, it builds to a notably chaotic crescendo—even for a September Sound 1. Remarkably strong—even for a September Sound 1.

The first ever Sound 1 outro develops around the Sound 1 ending/intro riff. A bliss theme develops and builds by way of Peter and the Wolf and Sound 1 teases into a strong B&C ending.
Pure melancholic trance until Sammy kicks up the tempo and shifts to dnb.

One of many titans of fall 01. Magner and Barber craft a bliss theme together, and then Barber begins to push the jam into the distinctive September 01 sound. It reaches a somewhat chaotic crescendo before breaking down into a Sound 1 intro.

The jam out of Boop stagnates in Boop territory for only a few minutes, before a complete breakdown. Thunderous rhythm from Allen and Brownie and background riffing from Barber set up the canvas on which Aron Magner paints his masterpiece. His synth lines are evocative, both simple and haunting, and he crafts a gorgeous atmosphere. The jam is very clearly in Buddha territory from the beginning of this theme, and seems to be heading toward the infrequently-jammed-into middle section, but after an adroit breakdown the band segues into the beginning.

The main jam explores the deepest pockets of type one imaginable. Excellent atmospheric texturing from Barber.

The funk jam is, for maybe the first time, the main attraction. Magner and Barber craft an infectious groovy theme from the very beginning. The second half is a bit more standard, but, since it's September 01, it’s still pretty great.

A superlative version, which breaks down after a melancholy theme and furtive crescendo. The buildup to the peak is gorgeously thematic, highlighted by Barber’s use of characteristic fall 01 muted distortion.

The first version without Mauricio and it’s executed brilliantly. Great psychedelic atmosphere in the first half that yields to symphonic excellence in the second. Arguably the beginning of the golden age of Munchkin Invasion.
More of a blissful venture than typical, the dubby Hope jam covers multiple themes before reaching Kamaole bliss.
The B&C jam covers a remarkable amount of ground for its short time stamp, getting into an extended passage of chaotic weirdness before culminating in triumphant Hope territory.
An uneven standalone version, with an absolutely transcendent passage towards the beginning.
Experimental and mellow, the jam has two distinct themes and peaks before settling into the Floes intro.

Magner crafts a spacey trance groove over the chugging riffs of the Frog Legs ending that the rest of the band quickly picks up on. A spectacular theme develops naturally around this groove before breaking down and resolving into a standard Run Like Hell jam. The Run Like Hell ending is explosive, even for the era.
A spooky Basis jam for this haunted lodge show. The jam builds up to speed and, rather than peaking, keeps pace and develops into a frenetic Shem-Rah intro.

Beginning with the mournful quality of a Eulogy intro, the jam quickly evolves into faster paced trance while still keeping its mournful qualities. Like the more famous movie jam from the previous night, there are multiple peaks, and it follows a similar formula—bliss peak, tense jam, breakdown, percussive/demented section, huge peak, type one. There’s some spectacular stuff hidden in here, and it deserves every bit as much recognition as the Koyaanisqatsi jam.
The jam stays in Vassilios territory for a while, developing a smooth-trance jam before breaking down into cacophony and rebuilding into a groove-oriented B&C intro.

It begins as an ordinary Waves jam, building in intensity and ferocity to a massive crescendo. However, as the intensity builds, the jam changes keys from F#m (Waves) to A major (RLH). The band drops the tempo simultaneously and seamlessly for the Run Like Hell ending.

Proceeds as a typical Basis jam, with moody atmospheric trance gradually building in intensity. Rather than shifting to the major key of the Basis peak, the band holds fast in this moody atmosphere as Sammy kicks up the tempo and signals the transition into Dribble.
A mellow yet morose trance jam develops out of Pygmy, breaking down and rebuilding into a decidedly more fast-paced Barber-led section. The build into Waves is some of the greatest Barber ever.

The jam begins as the standard fall 99 dub Waves exploration. The theme Magner locks into carries the first half of the jam until it breaks down and Sammy shifts from a dub groove to a more standard rock and roll style. The remainder of the jam is a Barber-led exploration of a Pygmy intro—probably the closest Pygmy has gotten to a true intro jam.

Epoch defining jungle. Magner’s synth sounds call to mind the coos of tropical birds. The band creates order around Sammy’s insane breakbeats, the very definition of controlled chaos. The effect is at once a hauntingly catchy atmosphere with inscrutable complexity. The jam covers a diverse territory and builds to a gorgeous ending.

A somber atmospheric jam augmented by a fantastic sound profile from Magner. Some classical piano yields to atmospheric trance in the first minutes. There is some excellent theme-building but nothing out of the ordinary for a Trooper jam until around 7:30 when Magner begins to creep in with the staccato “rabbit hole” synths. The jam takes on the quality of a trip through a haunted forest. At the 11 minute mark Magner breaks out the choir of angels patch and the trance synths. The jam sounds like it’s heading back towards Trooper until the final minute when it breaks for the Helicopters ending.

This is only the third Waves ever, and the first to be split.  The jam has all the makings of a standard early Waves rager, replete with Magner's 1998 style synths and Barber shredding, but the jam breaks down just shy of the eleven minute mark. The remainder of the Waves track is a mellow segue into Vassillios.
Powerful and dramatic, Magner soars early on this House Dog ending and Barber brings it home. Broken up into three pieces, this is one of the more creative uses of HDPF in 2.0.

An I-Man outro that deftly bridges the gap between the blissful I-Man ending and the tense Waves ending. The majority of the jam is a dub exploration, reaching some moments of "pirate trance" in the middle.

Magner holds remarkably close to the same theme throughout the jam. Ordinarily this might lead to staid or uninteresting improvisation, but he shifts the theme through different moods, allowing the jam to develop from somber to triumphant.

Magner is thoroughly in control of this jam, and his synth choices come through beautifully on the master. Around 7:15 he links up perfectly with Barber, and the theme they craft culminates in possibly the best Trooper intro ever.
Another gorgeous Mauricio version, this version might top even 3/11. Magner’s atmospheric synth choices characterize the jam, and Barber ultimately delivers a strong ending.

The second iteration of this section is less experimental than the first, but more focused. The band settles into a melancholy trance theme much more quickly, building up to a Mulberry’s middle fakeout in the middle. The jam rebuilds into a trance theme that gradually moves toward a breakbeat style as it approaches Spaga.
A Happy Dribble (the first since 12/30/99) with a gorgeous conclusion.
Fast-paced trance right out of the gate, it settles into a drawn-out and sinister theme before building back up to Confrontation.

Though it’s not the longest Astronaut of the year, it may very well be the most thematic. The groove is focused and thematic, and builds to a large, unconventionally blissful peak before returning to Astronaut.

Magner crafts an excellent theme around the dnb rhythm that builds to a triumphant crescendo, which culminates as Sammy shifts the rhythm very suddenly to a trance beat for a somewhat jarring transition into Run Like Hell.
The Morph outro begins as demented trance and moves to a melancholy, piano-heavy theme before returning to the Hot Air Balloon ending.

A very broad jam, beginning with some vocalizations, shifting into a standard Party Favor jam, and then departing for more experimental territory. There is a bliss theme which then breaks down into a tense shuffling passage and slowly rebuilds into a strong ending.
The jam is a fairly standard trance build until a percussive shift into dnb-adjacent territory. It holds space in Munchkin territory before finally segueing into the song.

The last Unspoken Rhyme for almost 15 years is unconventional: it quickly sheds typical fast-paced dnb in favor of relaxed, hypnotic dub. Excellent atmosphere, and a cool Phish-y segue into Magellan to boot.

The only non-Strobelights Dribble of the month. It begins with thunderous bass thumping and polyrhythmic drumming. Gradually, it settles into a trance rhythm, before building up and shifting to a blissful Confrontation ending.
The yin to 9/8’s yang. Like that version, this one has two fully fleshed-out themes. The first is a powerful Reactor jam, and the second is a slow-burn to the Ladies ending.
An absolutely relentless trance juggernaut with two peaks.
A groove-oriented bliss jam emerges from the Shimmy outro. After some type one, it returns to dnb and builds back to Bazaar Escape.

Driving trance that quickly leaves behind the distinct rhythm of Pygmy and heads for four-on-the-floor territory. It settles down, gradually, into a blissful and expansive jam that yields a smooth Aceetobee intro. Gorgeous riffs from Barber.

Arguably marks the beginning of a really strong period for Munchkin, where it is given the B&C treatment—i.e., every version is given a sinister theme before returning to type one territory. This is an especially strong version.
Hypnotic and fast-paced trance, the jam fakes out the Reactor ending before shifting seamlessly into Crickets territory. Massive peak.
In contrast to the jam into Crickets, the jam out is very mellow and restrained. It settles into a dub passage before building up to The Big Happy.

A grimy Magner trance vehicle. It quickly settles into some airy space, and Sammy begins to increase the tempo rapidly. Magner utilizes the Gates of Hell and Barber uses the same psychedelic distortion effect that characterizes the Svenghali jam. The effect is fantastic, and the jam builds to a solid Munchkin ending.

The jam starts off as a standard blissful trance jam. Magner makes contributions on the choir of angels synths over Sammy’s feather-light trance rhythm. Barber takes the lead and soon delivers one of the most gorgeous themes I’ve heard in Munchkin. The theme comes to a head, before breaking down and settling into a cool groove, building back up into a driving trance rhythm about a minute later. Barber takes lead once again for a brilliant build into Confrontation, culminating in what might be the strongest Confrontation peak ever.
Haunting digital trance in the vein of Sound 1, a furious percussive breakdown, and a sinister build into Shimmy. Absolutely 100% evil the entire way through.
Explores the spaces between light and dark, and yields as strong a peak as the song has ever seen.
Absolutely brain-melting, breakneck trance. A short jam, but an absolute firecracker.

More ambient and atmospheric in the first minutes than the typical Shelby Rose jam. Sammy teases a potential segue into 4xfloor trance, but quickly reverts to breakbeats. The rest of the jam is fairly standard.
Simultaneously playful and restrained, the Shimmy trance breaks down into a rollicking Ladies intro.

After several exploratory mid-verse jams in the fall, Run Like Hell is finally segued out of the mid-verse jam. The jam is pretty and forceful, a Magner-led trance jaunt that builds to a huge Barber peak into Helicopters.

Subverting expectations, the Rhyme jam begins as a steady rock groove rather than traditional dnb. The jam starts off poppy and blissful, before building to a crescendo and dropping into M.E.M.P.H.I.S.
The Crickets funk gradually leaves behind funk territory for a major-key trance rock jam. Huge crescendo and smooth segue into the beginning of Shelby.

Sammy’s drum beat remains the only real constant, never straying too far from Don, but the rest of the band move through a variety of moods and themes, at first tense and uncertain, then moody, then more triumphant. The jam seems to be heading toward a massive Run Like Hell ending until Barber suddenly signals the segue into Helicopters.

The jam builds up to a triumphant trance crescendo that breaks down into an eerie soundscape. Magner uses the flute patch concurrently with his drone synths to a pretty neat effect. The jam continues further into spooky territory as Magner begins using a demonic vocoder effect, and the jam steadily builds to a haunting crescendo as it reaches Shimmy territory.

Settles into a type two theme almost immediately. Barber’s theme is so simple and effective, and perfectly complements Magner’s atmosphere. A breakdown and more tense theme lead into the Hot Air Balloon intro.
The rare Grass is Green outro finds a life of its own before Sammy kicks up the tempo and introduces the breakbeats, from which point an excellent Svenghali intro develops.
A pretty standard dnb vehicle until Sammy begins to signal the transition into Crickets. A masterfully executed segue into Crickets develops.

The first Dribble after the monumental 3/31 version utilizes some of the percussion effects that defined that version. The first half of the jam is smooth and silky, with some excellent interplay between Magner and Barber, and decently removed from Dribble territory. After a lengthy dub passage, the jam abruptly returns to Dribble territory before breaking down into a drawn out bliss theme. Superb version, and completely under the radar.

In an era positively overflowing with excellent dnb jams, this one still manages to stand out as one of the best, and for good reason. There are two distinct themes, the first a more traditional dark dnb build and the second a more experimental vehicle.

Perhaps the first important Crickets first jam. The jam weaves in and out of the Crickets theme, never venturing too far outside of it, but beginning to push the envelope a bit, until Magner delivers a decisive synth line at 12:30 to signal the move towards the peak.

There are several minutes of type one Hot Air Balloon shredding, which immediately segues into Dribble territory. Rather than segueing directly into the ending, the jam breaks down into a slow, dubby groove. This passage lasts several minutes before the band even begins to build back up to Dribble. A totally unique take on the Dribble ending.
Patient and evil, the sinister type one gives way to a triumphant major-mode theme before returning to Shimmy territory.

The first jam takes a turn into distinctly dark territory before a haunting build to the peak.

The outro yields to an excellent funk groove, with Magner delivering an infectious line on the flute patch. This smoothly transitions into Mulberry’s.

There is nothing conventional about this jam. The composition organically gives way to Phish style Barber-heavy jamming which reaches a peak shortly after the nine minute mark. An early ambient trance jam develops and plays out over several minutes before resolving into more standard grooves. A gorgeous Barber-led bliss section leads back into the peak.
A banner version, beginning as an ambient trance jam and building to a powerful, percussive crescendo.

The standard blissful Don trance gives way to a more tense Magner-led theme within the first few minutes of the jam. Barber takes more of a commanding role around 12:30 and the jam settles down considerably into spacey atmosphere. The build-up back to the Don ending is extremely patient and thematic

An unusually long mid-verse jam, which incorporates atypical percussive patterns and repetitive trance synths and vocal samples from Magner. It has a darkly foreboding mood, shifting to bliss territory as it returns to the second verse.

The jam features thunderous percussion and abrasive Magner synth effects. It stays in this territory as Magner returns to more melodic synths, and the jam builds up to a thrilling crescendo that comes crashing into the middle section of I-Man.

The main jam is spectacular, and vaguely sinister. Various themes build off of each other, while Sammy’s drum work keeps the jam moving. After a small breakdown, Magner develops an excellent theme on the trance synths that builds in intensity for the rest of the jam, and a couple minutes later he begins to incorporate the Gates of Hell. Paradoxically, the key change comes shortly after. The jam builds to a phenomenal Basis peak.

A catchy groove based around the apple butter toast riff soon yields a more uplifting Dribble jam than usual. It stays pretty removed from Dribble territory, returning to the Dribble hits only once, after a blissful crescendo. From here the jam enters another bliss passage, breaking down even further. Shortly after this, Sammy reintroduces the Bazaar Escape hits, and the tempo picks up as the jam reenters Bazaar territory. Great build back into the hey hey heys,
Drawn out jamming with multiple distinct themes, including a Waves dub and a drawn out and developed Plums intro.

The jam begins with a fantastic, clean jungle theme. Barber’s playing grows increasingly chaotic over the backdrop of a Magner soundscape. The jam grows tenser until a breakdown, as Sammy’s beat transitions smoothly from jungle into a housey rock groove while Magner maintains continuity with his previous theme. The groove soon becomes distinctly more playful, not unlike a M.E.M.P.H.I.S. intro. Barber shifts to the muted distortion shortly afterward to great effect. It leaves this playful theme only in the final seconds of the track, building in tempo rapidly for the transition into Hot Air Balloon.

The jam gets off to a frenetic start, and explores a wider variety of different ideas than typical. It begins with breakbeats, and toes the line between a groove theme and a dnb jam. It settles into a groove at the track change, and begins to build up to a Basis intro. Magner uses a harsh digital synth to great effect, and Barber hits some cool riffs.

The jam begins with some mellow ambient waves from Magner and muted distortion from Barber in a melancholy theme. Pretty soon Magner introduces the flute patch to great effect. This theme breaks down, and Magner introduces a trance lead that he builds over several minutes. The back half of this jam is incredible, with Magner and Barber trading lead around this theme and building to a great ending.

Gradually ebbing away from Trooper territory, the jam lands in a catchy theme that lasts for a few minutes before picking up in tempo and shifting towards a breakbeat rhythm. The jam ultimately transitions with smoothness into an inverted Overture.

The Spaga jam begins in familiar territory, but Magner soon latches onto an incredible theme that he holds for several minutes, featuring some of his most expressive synth work. The flute patch helps settle the jam down, and it begins to rebuild into a more driving psychedelic groove. The jam segues into Floes masterfully without any need to slow down.
A spectacular first jam, probably the best so far and one of the best ever. Excellent theme-building from Barber.

The jam explores a very cool dnb theme until breaking down and rebuilding into a mellow, blissful trance theme. Barber lays down some gorgeous jazzy riffs, and the jam builds up to a kind of wall-of-sound crescendo that segues masterfully into the chase section of Jigsaw Earth.

The Pygmy jam is a sinister trance vehicle right out of the gate, building to a brain-melting and evil crescendo that shifts to bliss in the final minute of the track and results in an excellent Confrontation ending.
A masterful jam, beginning unassumingly and building to the most powerful and sinister Crickets peak ever played.
The first half of the jam is solid, if a bit restrained, but the second half, in which Magner takes the reins, is excellent and explosive.
The Crickets trance jam immediately gets into sinister territory and explores a type two theme before building up to a fantastic Confrontation peak.
An expansive trance jam that settles into a hypnotic groove. Magner holds down his theme all the way through the jam as Barber takes on a more prominent role and shifts back into Hot Air Balloon.
A Barber-led jam in the beginning, which gradually yields to an atonal trance breakdown.

The jam stays Type I, but is played with great passion and energy, as the band was likely excited to drop the CWB Opera on the unsuspecting Cleveland audience. After a minute of standard Plan B jamming, Sammy goes into a double-time feel and things get weird. Sounding similar to a demented Magellan jam, they build up the intensity for a great Plan B peak. This Plan B served as a great kickoff for a well-played CWB opera with a good amount of improv.
The first jam begins in tense territory, moves through a chaotic breakdown and builds to a monster of a peak.
Simple Magner grooves characterize the first theme. The middle portion of the jam features excellent Barber/Magner interplay, and builds to a strong peak not always seen in Overture jams.

The jam stays close to blissful B&C territory for the first several minutes, stretching and spacing this theme out as far as it will go.
